title: Dots and vowels
hook: dots and vowel marks were added later to help new readers

segments.voice: Yesterday, mushaf: Uthman's copies, one standard sent out to the cities. Your line was one text, many cities. Did the world feel a little smaller? Day three hundred eighteen.

Picture three Arabic letters: ba, ta, tha. In a modern mushaf they have exactly the same shape, a little boat. The only difference is the dots: one below for ba, two above for ta, three above for tha. Now imagine the dots gone. That's close to what the earliest copies looked like: the bones of the words, with the reader supplying the rest from what they'd learned by ear. Today: dots and vowels.
screen: `BA, TA, THA: ONE SHAPE.` → `ONLY THE DOTS DIFFER.` → `NOW TAKE THE DOTS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Early Arabic writing was a kind of shorthand. Many letters shared a shape, and the dots that tell them apart were used sparingly. Short vowels weren't written at all. For the first Muslims that wasn't a problem: the Qur'an lived in their mouths, learned from teachers, and the page was a reminder of what they already knew. But Islam spread fast, to people whose first language wasn't Arabic, and mistakes in recitation began. Tradition credits a scholar of Basra, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, in the first Islamic century, with the first vowel marks: colored dots, often red, placed above, below or beside a letter to show its sound. Later, in the time of the governor al-Hajjaj, scholars are said to have added the dots that tell similar letters apart more fully. And in the next century, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad of Basra, who also mapped the meters of Arabic poetry, gave the vowels the small shapes still used today: a slanting stroke above, a tiny curl like a waw, a stroke below. Sources tell the details differently, and early manuscripts show some dots from very early on. But the direction is clear. Nobody changed the text. The marks were added around it, the way you might add pronunciation guides to a poem for a new reader. Some scholars at the time disliked writing anything extra inside the mushaf. In the end the community accepted the marks, because they served the recitation that had been passed down. Every dot is a kindness to a learner.
screen: `THE SAME SHAPE, DIFFERENT DOTS` · `A PAGE THAT REMINDED, NOT TAUGHT` · `RED DOTS FOR VOWELS` · `MARKS ADDED AROUND THE TEXT`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the dots above the letters. If you have a mushaf or an app, open any page and just look. Don't try to read. Find the dots: one, two, three, above and below. Find the tiny vowel strokes. Notice how much of the page is made of these small marks, placed there for someone learning. If there's no page in front of you, picture ba, ta and tha, three little boats told apart only by their dots. Rest your eyes. The bell holds the time.
Dots and vowels. The marks added to the Qur'an's script in its first centuries, so new readers could recite it rightly. Today's word.
Your line: marks for the reader. Today, add one small mark that helps whoever comes after you: a clear label, a note, a patient word of instruction for someone new. Day three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Muslims today read from copies with full dots and vowel marks, and learners, especially those who didn't grow up with Arabic, rely on those marks to recite correctly.

fork.setup: you teach the Qur'an in Basra. new Muslims who didn't grow up with Arabic keep misreading the vowels. what do you do?
options: change the words to easier ones.
add small marks to show the sounds.
fork.reveal: tradition says that's exactly what Abu al-Aswad did: colored dots for the vowels, with the words untouched.

original.note: Arabic: vowel marking, the small strokes that show short vowels. the dots that tell letters apart are called i'jam.

trapdoor: what you thought: Arabic script always looked like this.
what it means: dots and vowel marks added over the first centuries to help new readers recite correctly.
what a scholar hears: i'jam and tashkil, credited in tradition to Abu al-Aswad, the circle of al-Hajjaj and al-Khalil, though early manuscripts already show some dots.

notes: Attributions (Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, d. c. 69 AH; Nasr ibn Asim and Yahya ibn Ya'mur under al-Hajjaj; al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, d. c. 170 AH) follow the traditional account; sources vary. Confirm.
Early manuscripts with sparse consonant dots: a general statement; confirm.
